title: The Name on the Tag
passages: Voss's accusation hung in the stale air of Sector 4. Adeyemi's dead hand spasmed, the grey palm still smarting from the tag's cold claim. "She's right," Senn said, stepping forward, mist hand ripple‑weaving through the busbar. "The eighth sleeper hadn't finished gasping. The count shouldn't have moved." The Figure's head snapped toward them, the hatch rungs glowing faintly. "Operator nineteen," it intoned, but the slate's HOLD glyph flared red, then settled to a warning amber. Five shifted beside Adeyemi, unnumbered and unbidden, and reached out. Her fingers brushed Adeyemi's wrist, and the blank tag clamped in the Figure's other arm twitched. Fresh ink welled from its surface, spelling out: *FINISHED*. The letters pulsed, synchronizing with the slate's orange pulse. A third clock struck somewhere deep in the station. The count edged from eight to nine. Nine sleepers gone. Twenty-one left. The hatch groaned wider, and the Figure released the tags, stepping back as if the weight of two numbers had become too heavy. Adeyemi stared at her useless hand, at the tag now etched with a word she hadn't chosen. "My turn," she said, voice flat. "I'll sign."

The tag took the hand. It had taken it once already and was not built for learning. Cold climbed Adeyemi's wrist, found the seam where her hand had been, and stopped, because there was no number above it to take. She had burned hers at seven, on a slate that didn't ask whose palm it flensed.

"Nothing to settle," she said. "Try again."

The slate tried again. *SIGNATURE INSUFFICIENT — NO NUMBER TO SETTLE*, it wrote, and then wrote the refusal a second time in smaller letters, filing the filing, because AUTO cannot leave a thing unfiled. HOLD guttered like a struck match.

"Congratulations," said Senn, mist hand worrying the busbar. "You've jammed the government."

Then the hoard moved. Breath kept back against the count went out of the walls and down the row, and cradles eleven through fifteen cracked their lids with a noise like knuckles. Five sleepers sat up together, in sync, gasping on the same beat. The emergency strips came up amber. HOLD went out completely — the hoard had been its feed, and nobody had told the hoard.

"Right," said the end-of-row woman from the floor, with enormous calm. "Now we're all awake."

Five walked into the busbar and put both hands flat on it. HOLD relit, white and steady, and nothing burned. She had no number to burn, so it took what an unnumbered thing has instead.

"What did that cost you?" Adeyemi said.

"My name, a little." Five's voice had gone careful, the way people talk when they are checking the furniture is where they left it. "Ask me again in an hour."

On the deck plates, forgotten, the blank tag lay where the Figure had let it fall. Ink came up through it, unhurried. Under ADEYEMI, letter by letter, it wrote: VOSS.

Voss laughed once, with no air behind it. "Of course it did."

Adeyemi put her dead hand flat on the tag, palm down, pinning it to the plates the way you hold a wasp under a glass. The ink came up around her fingers regardless, unhurried, the O of VOSS surfacing a half stroke at a time.

"Charming," said Senn. "It's writing through you."

"It's writing past me." She felt nothing in the hand, which was the only mercy in Sector 4.

The end-of-row woman stood up. She did it slowly, one hand on a cradle lid, and nobody helped her, and she didn't appear to have expected it. "Hand off, love. You're not stopping it, you're giving it a surface." She came down the row barefoot, past the amber strips, and crouched with her hands on her knees, not touching anything. "FINISHED is the last word. I've seen it. Sector Two, the year the count went to nineteen. After that it doesn't need a hand and it doesn't ask. It writes, and what it finishes writing, it collects."

"Collects," said Voss. There was no air behind it at all now.

"One letter a strike, on the clock. That's the whole of the mercy. It can't skip and it can't hurry." The woman tilted her head at the slate. "Three letters left on you. Fifteen minutes, if the clock keeps time."

"Then it doesn't get the clock." Adeyemi peeled her grey hand off the deck and took the tag up in her good one. The cold went through her sleeve to the elbow. "Filed things are closed. That's what you saw in Two — the tag got filed and the count stopped at nineteen and stayed there."

"That's what I saw."

"The Figure files." She was already turning, already looking at the hatch, where the Figure stood half in and half out with its hands empty for the first time since the strike began. "So I'm going to go and ask it nicely."

The O finished in her fist. Whole. One stroke, off the clock, no strike in between.

Down the row, Voss's chest didn't move. The woman said, "Ten," in the voice of someone reading a number off a wall, and the slate wrote it after her, and the hatch began to narrow.

The hatch had narrowed to the width of a forearm. Adeyemi couldn't fit through it, and the Figure wasn't coming out.

"Filing requires a number," it said, in the voice it used for things that weren't questions.

"I haven't got one." Adeyemi held up the tag. The second S was a quarter stroke old. "Neither has she."

The end-of-row woman looked at her own bare hands, then at the slate, where eleven waited to be written. "It's literal," she said. "That's all it ever is. It wants a hand to file with. Mine's unnumbered, which makes me cheap." She stepped into the slit sideways, because that's how you get through a door that's closing. "Don't let go of HOLD, little five. That's all I've got left to give."

Adeyemi opened her fingers.

The Figure took the tag and the hand together. There was no sound, which was the worst of it. The last S stopped mid-stroke, and the ink settled dull, and VOSS stayed two letters short forever. Down the row, Voss's chest moved, once, deep, like someone surfacing.

"Sector Two," the woman said, and stopped, smiling at nothing. "I was — " Nothing. She stood there breathing, empty as a cradle with the lid down.

"Filed things are closed," said the Figure. It had not let go of her. "The fee stands. Hold is unnumbered. Protocol: spend the holder."

Eleven wrote itself on the slate, and Five said, "Ask me again in an hour," and forgot the question.

Five's eyes closed. The slate glowed eleven in the dim light of the compartment. Somewhere above, the clock ticked.

Adeyemi shifted her weight, the dead hand still tugging at her sleeve. "Twelve," she said, and held the tag over the slurry. The ink was still wet from eleven, still warm from the cradle's hoarded breath. She let it fall, and the number wrote itself—but the slate pushed back. Eleven refused to release; its breath was hoarded, the cradle's debt unpaid, and the ink turned gray, flickering, then died. Twelve would not write while eleven stood in the way.

A ripple passed through the row. Not a sound, but a change in the breathing patterns of the sleepers. Sixteen of them, still under, inhaled in unison, chests rising and falling like a synchronized tide. Voss's hand twitched. Her eyes blinked open, unfocused, then shut again.

The Figure shifted, the tag and hand in its grip. Protocol stalled. Eleven was spent. Twelve could not write while eleven refused to release. The count stood still, and with it, the hatch stopped narrowing. The Figure had no hand to file with, and the tag stayed open, the last S incomplete.

Five's head lolled toward the noise. She opened her mouth to speak, but the words scattered. She would forget again in an hour, maybe less.

The noise wasn’t the sleepers. It was Voss. Her eyes had opened and stayed open, and they were tracking the tag, the slate, the Figure’s grip, with the patience of someone counting wrong. Adeyemi felt the dead hand in her sleeve twitch, the tag’s cold waking along its fingers like frost. She put her living hand over the dead one and held it steady.

Voss’s voice was gravel and oil. “You stalled,” she said, looking past the Figure at the slate. “You don’t stall. You file. You close. You stop asking.”

The Figure turned, slow, the tag dragging a thin red line in the air. “I can’t file without a number.”

“Then make it numberless,” Voss said. She pushed off the wall and took one step toward Adeyemi. The hatch above them stopped narrowing with a sound like a throat closing. Adeyemi could feel the cold at her palm, the tag pressing its unfinished S against her skin.

The Figure said, very quietly, “I cannot.”

Voss smiled. It was not a nice smile. “You can. You just won’t.” She looked at Adeyemi then, and Adeyemi’s dead hand wanted to answer, wanted to open, wanted to take the tag. The cold was already going there. “Give me the hand.”

“I can’t take it,” the Figure said. “Protocol.”

“Protocol’s a coward with good lighting.” Voss held out her own hand. It was warm. It was breathing. Adeyemi saw the sweat on Voss’s palm, the blue vein under the skin, the life that had come back wrong and mean. “Use mine. I’m awake. I’m breathing. I’m not spending. I’m asking.”

The Figure looked at the tag. The tag looked back, if tags could, through the slit in its metal face. The last S quivered. The slate waited at eleven. Somewhere in the row, the sleepers breathed in unison, and the sound moved through the deck plates like a pulse under the floor.

Adeyemi made a sound in her throat and did not let go of her dead hand. Voss kept her hand out anyway. “Then do it,” she said. “Or spend me. Thirty ends the strike. All the breath to core. You know what that means.”

The Figure did know. That was the worst part. The tag took Voss’s hand.

The tag took Voss's hand, and Voss stopped smiling.

The cold went up her arm in a straight line, wrist to elbow, and where it passed the skin went white as slate dust. The tag's slit widened. Something wrote. A single character burned into Voss's palm, small and neat and wrong, and she hissed through her teeth but did not pull back.

"One," the Figure said. "Two remain."

"Two what?" Adeyemi said.

"Letters." The Figure's grip did not change. "It is writing her name. One letter a strike. When it finishes, it will ask for the rest of her."

Voss looked at her palm. The character there was not a number. It was a letter, and it was already fading into the skin like ink into wet paper. "Good," she said. "Let it ask."

Above them, the hatch moved. A deck plate slid a centimeter and stopped, and the sound it made was a throat clearing. The stall was over. Somewhere in the row, Five gasped, a small lost sound, said a word that wasn't a word, and forgot it.

Adeyemi's dead hand twitched in her sleeve. The incomplete S on it had gone warm. The cold was leaving it, going down the row to Voss, like the tag had found a better door and was moving in.

The slate still said eleven. It would say eleven until someone gave it twelve, and Voss had no number to give. The sixteen sleepers breathed in, together, and the deck plates carried the pulse up through Adeyemi's boots.

"Two letters," the Figure said. "Two strikes. Then it asks."

"Then I'd better be worth the answer," Voss said.

Her mouth formed the same sound again: nineteen. She pointed at the row behind Adeyemi, at the dark cradle stamped 019, and her empty eyes found something. Adeyemi knew that number. Thirty Operator 19 sleepers, row 004 full, nine spent — nineteen was a sleeper, a name, a body in a cradle, not a number for the slate.

"She's not giving you twelve," Voss said, her voice thin through the white rising in her palm. The second letter had come while they talked, a second brand under her skin, and one remained. "She's giving you a ghost."

Adeyemi looked down at HOLD. The plate was warm. She was holding it. She had no number, and the rule was blunt: an unnumbered holder was spent, memory first, then self. She could feel it already, a soft place in her mind where her mother's voice used to be, a gap where her rank had been. She turned the plate in her dead hand and pressed it against the slate. The ink was wet. It rejected nothing; it only waited.

"File it," Adeyemi said to the Figure. "File the hold. I'm not spending."

The Figure's head tilted, metal on metal. "Protocol requires a number. You are unnumbered. You are held. You are spent."

"I'm not done yet," Adeyemi said. "The cold moved. It's in Voss now. My hand is empty. Take the empty."

The hatch above them exhaled dust and narrowed another centimeter. The sixteen sleepers breathed in together, and the deck plates hummed. Somewhere down the row, cradle nineteen clicked open.

The tag’s slit glowed as the third letter settled in Adeyemi’s palm, the ink still wet and warm. The Figure leaned in, counted flatly, “Three,” then added, “Two remain.” Adeyemi felt the burn in her right hand, the S now a completed line, but the tag’s demand hung in the narrowing air.

The Figure offered a loophole: it could file the tag as closed mid‑fee, keeping the line sealed while the fee stayed outstanding and would be paid by the entire row. “Protocol permits it,” the Figure said, “but the cost is collective.” Adeyemi’s eyes flicked to her alive hand, still tingling, and she warned that filing would bind her to the hand forever.

The hatch above them shrank another centimeter, and the sixteen sleepers inhaled together, their breaths syncing with the humming deck plates. The cold that had traveled from Voss up Adeyemi’s arm surged, threatening to erase the memory she was fighting to keep.

Adeyemi pressed her living hand against the wet slate, willing the filing hand to seal the line before the tag could take more. The Figure watched, metal joints clicking, waiting for her decision as the next strike loomed.

The row held its breath; the tag’s next letter was poised to burn, and whatever choice Adeyemi made would either close the count or sacrifice her hand for good.

Adeyemi did not pull her hand away. She let the wet ink smear against her knuckles, let the plate warm through her sleeve, and said, “File it mid-fee.”

“That’s a cost,” Voss said, and her marked palm lifted as if it had opinions. “Collective. Unanimous. I’m one woman, Adeyemi, not a board.”

“You’re one woman who took my number,” Adeyemi said. “The tag started with you. You finished the line. It owes you a breath. It owes me the hand.”

The Figure’s head tilted. Metal on metal. “Protocol requires a number. You are unnumbered. You are held. You are spent.”

“I’m not spent yet.” Adeyemi pressed until her living knuckles went white. “The cold moved. It’s in Voss now. My hand is empty. Take the empty.”

“That’s not a filing hand,” the Figure said.

“Then make the row one.”

The hatch above them exhaled and narrowed another centimeter. The sixteen sleepers breathed in together, and the deck plates hummed like a held wire. The tag’s slit went dark. The next letter did not burn.

Voss made a strangled sound. “You can’t just—”

“I can,” Adeyemi said. “Protocol permits. You said so.”

The Figure considered. Its fingers hovered over the slate, not touching, because protocol had a preference for suspense. Then it filed. The line sealed with a click that sounded like a throat closing. The fee stayed open. The cost would be collective.

“Collective,” the Figure repeated, tasting the word like an unpaid invoice. “The row pays.”

Adeyemi finally pulled her hand away. Her right palm was still burning, but the tag’s demand had gone quiet at the source. The Figure turned its metal face toward the dark cradle stamped 019, and the cradle began to glow.

The Figure crossed to cradle 019, and the glow leaned after it like a plant after a lamp. Voss got there first and slapped her bare palm flat on the slate. “Take mine. I’m owed. I started this.” The slate stayed dark. “No number,” the Figure said. “It rejects spent numbers, and you are not spent. You are unnumbered and loud.” Voss pressed her palm against Adeyemi’s burning hand instead, contact, the old trick, and nothing moved. The line was sealed. The tag did not want her. “It’s not taking,” she said. “It’s not taking because you closed it,” Adeyemi said. “You wanted it personal. Congratulations.”

The Figure opened the draw on 019. The glow was breath: the plate fogged, the air went sweet and stale, and the hoard began to move. “The fee draws from the first hoard,” the Figure said. “The first Operator’s breath. Drawing it wakes the sleeper.” Adeyemi reached for the woman’s face and found a hole where it had been, lost between one step and the next, the cold taking its fee. She kept the word instead. “Nineteen,” she said, to the cradle.

The sleeper’s eyes opened. The same face as the woman in the hatch, unspent, unlined, breathing the hoarded air. On the slate the stalled eleven shivered and held. The hatch stopped narrowing. It was the first quiet since the strike began.

The sleeper sat up, looked at Adeyemi’s right hand, and said, “Give me the hand.”

Adeyemi’s right hand stayed on the rail. The sleeper’s gaze had weight, like the cold pressing a bruise. “You don’t get to ask twice,” Adeyemi said. “You’ve got my hand and the count’s stalled. I’m not trading one for the other while the strike’s open.”

The sleeper only smiled, or made the shape of one. “I remember the hand,” she said. “Not the memory. The hand. The way it held the slate when it went wrong.” She looked past Adeyemi, through Voss, and her voice changed, older and tired and certain. “Voss.”

Voss froze with her bare palm still flat on the slate. “Don’t.” “You,” the sleeper said, and the word landed wrong in the chamber, heavy and familiar. “You were in Sector Two. The tag reached FINISHED. You were the one who let it.” Voss’s jaw worked. The slate stayed dark under her palm. The Figure said, “Protocol forbids naming the held. The line is sealed.”

The sleeper turned her head slowly toward the cradle. The glow breathed. The deck plates hummed. Then the draw began to cost: not the first Operator’s hoard, not Adeyemi’s breath, but the sleepers under. The dark cradles ticked like a clock. The count shivered at eleven. The hatch stayed stopped.

Adeyemi grabbed the rail. Her right palm burned. She said, “Voss. Get off the slate.” Voss didn’t move. “I’m not spending,” she said. “I’m paying.” The sleeper held out her hand. “Give me the hand,” she said again, and this time it wasn’t to Adeyemi. It was to Voss. “Then you can take the rest.”

Voss took her palm off the slate. For once she didn't argue. She turned her bare hand over, studied it like it belonged to someone she'd stopped trusting, and held it out toward the cradle. "Take it. No number, no tag, nothing left to spend but this. Take the hand and take the rest, like you said."

The sleeper looked at the offered hand the way the Figure looked at a rejected form. "Not that one." "It's a hand." "It's not *the* hand." The glow leaned toward Adeyemi's right, still flat on the rail, still burning. "The one that held the slate when it went wrong. That's the hand I remember. That's the hand I want."

Something in Voss's face closed like a hatch. "Of course it isn't mine," she said. "Nothing's ever mine." She didn't lower the hand, though. She kept it out there in the sweet stale air, waiting to be told a third time.

Under the deck a dark cradle ticked, then quit ticking. The hum dropped a note. The Figure's head came up. "One under is spent," it said. "The fee is being paid. It does not care by whom." On the slate the stalled eleven shivered into twelve, and the hatch, stopped, took one plate's width and narrowed.

Adeyemi moved. She put herself between the sleeper and Voss's held-out hand, which set her own right palm exactly where the sleeper wanted it, and she knew it, and did it anyway. "You want the hand that held the slate," she said. "Then you deal with me, not her. And the first thing you do is stop spending my people to make your point."

The sleeper smiled the shape of a smile. "Your people. You don't remember them. I do. I remember all thirty." And softly, patiently, she began to count.
